paras: The lynching of Chris Davis took place in Athens, Ohio, on the night of November 20-21, 1881, when a mob took Davis, a Black man described as a "mulatto," from the county jail and hanged him from a Hocking River bridge. Davis was being held on a charge of raping and beating with an ax an elderly widow near Albany, Ohio. A coroner's jury blamed "parties unknown," Albany women endorsed the hanging, and papers North and South debated it.

In early November 1881 a news brief reported that Mrs. Lucinda "Tuckley," a widow near Albany in Athens County, had been "horribly maltreated by a negro," and that neighbors threatened to lynch her jailed assailant. Later accounts named her Lucinda Luckey and the accused as Davis, who according to a Memphis report had tended her farm for some years. The papers accused him of breaking in at night, raping her and striking her with an ax, dating the attack anywhere from October 29 to November 5.
Because of lynching threats he was moved to the Chillicothe jail. When the excitement seemed to have died down he was returned to Athens to go before the grand jury.

On Sunday night, November 20, men from Albany, about ten miles away, rode into Athens and posted guards at the houses of officials so that no alarm could be given. Several men gained entry to the jail by pretending to deliver a captured horse thief, then seized Sheriff Warden. Finding no keys, they broke the lock of his cell with a sledge.

The men led Davis with a rope around his neck four blocks to the bridge at the south edge of town. According to a Cincinnati Gazette dispatch, he was promised a return to jail "to be dealt with by law" if he confessed, and he said, "I'm the man." The men gave him three minutes to pray, then threw him from the bridge; the fall of about nine feet broke his neck, and his body was found there in the morning.

The first dispatch said the unmasked mob would be arrested, and the coroner opened an inquest that day. According to the Marietta Register, the verdict was that Davis died "at the hands of parties unknown, although the Sheriff swore to the identities of several." No report of any arrest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

In Albany, which a December 3 dispatch said was believed to have furnished the lynchers, a meeting of women adopted resolutions without dissent. The resolutions declared that Davis had "met a just and timely fate" and pledged to oppose prosecution of anyone involved.

The story first spread through two Cincinnati specials: a Times-Star dispatch on the seizure and hanging, and a Gazette dispatch on the confession at the bridge. Dailies from Wheeling to New York and Washington carried them on November 22 and 23, some headlined "at Albany," and reprints reached Mississippi and Texas by month's end.

Ohio Democratic weeklies largely approved. The Somerset Press wrote that "the lynchers have rid the country of a brute," and the Eaton Democrat hoped no jury would convict anyone in the lynching of "the black fiend and scoundrel Davis." The Perrysburg Journal called it "one of the most skillfully planned and executed lynchings on record." The Spirit of Democracy used it to mock Republican Athens and its "lovers of Negroes," calling the hanging "a Northern Outrage."

In Washington, the Republican National Republican paired the case with the Durand, Wisconsin, lynching and said the promise made at the bridge made the Athens affair "all the more disgraceful." Southern papers took it up as a sectional point: the Maysville Bulletin said it "shows a bad state of society over there," and the Jackson Clarion mocked northern papers "shocked" by it.

The wire and two later items called the mob unmasked; three Ohio papers described masked men. Its size was given as about twenty, about thirty, thirty-two, thirty or forty, and about fifty men. Two later Ohio accounts dated the lynching to the night of November 21, but the Athens dispatch of November 21 reported it as having happened "last night."

bases: A mob took Davis, jailed on an assault charge, from the Athens jail after overpowering the sheriff and hanged him from a bridge over the Hocking River (A10, A14, A30).

Davis was hanged by a mob numbered at twenty to fifty men who seized him from the sheriff's custody, without lawful authority, to punish an alleged rape and assault (A10, A14, A34, A35); the coroner found death 'at the hands of parties unknown' (A38).

Independent reports (the Cincinnati Times-Star and Gazette specials, A11 and A12, and separate Ohio accounts, A14, A30, A34) agree that a mob took Davis from the Athens jail and hanged him from the Hocking River bridge.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Times-Star wire
accounts.gist: Davis was hanged by a mob 'last night'; the sheriff was overpowered and the cell broken; the body was found on the Hocking bridge in the morning; the mob was not masked and would be arrested.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Gazette special (the mob's version of the hanging)
accounts.gist: At the bridge Davis was promised a return to jail if he confessed, said "I'm the man," and was given three minutes to pray before being thrown off.

accounts.label: Ohio weekly accounts
accounts.gist: Thirty to forty (or thirty-two, or about fifty) men from the Albany area gained entry with a horse-thief ruse, guarded officials' houses, broke the cell lock with a sledge and led Davis four blocks to the bridge.

accounts.label: Der Westbote (German)
accounts.gist: Thirty to forty masked men demanded the prisoner at about 1 a.m.; the sheriff refused and was thrown down, and his wife, upstairs, threw down the keys.

accounts.label: Marietta Register (via Spirit of Democracy)
accounts.gist: About thirty unmasked men; the coroner's verdict named 'parties unknown' though the sheriff swore to several identities.

framing.detail: Dailies ran the Times-Star and Gazette specials under heads such as 'Hanged by a Mob', 'A Negro Lynched at Albany, O.' and 'An Unavailing Confession'.
The Somerset Press said the lynchers 'rid the country of a brute'; the Eaton Democrat hoped no jury would convict any of them.
The National Republican, in 'Law or License?', said the broken promise at the bridge made the affair 'all the more disgraceful'.
The Spirit of Democracy mocked Republican Athens, calling the lynching 'a Northern Outrage', while describing Davis as having 'brutally assaulted' Mrs. Luckey.
Southern papers in Maysville and Jackson, Miss., used the case to answer northern papers that said lynching occurred only in the South.
